gloss_terse: Splendor, majesty, or honor; the awe-inspiring radiance of God, royalty, or personal dignity and distinction.
gloss_readable: A poetic term evoking the visible, almost tangible radiance that surrounds God or a king. In worship contexts it pairs naturally with hadar ('beauty') to describe the overwhelming grandeur of the LORD (1 Chr 29:11; Ps 21:5). The multilingual evidence confirms this pairing: German renders it Majestaet and Pracht, Spanish esplendor and majestad, all clustering around royal brilliance. Yet the word can also denote a more personal dignity or honor conferred on an individual, as when Moses transfers some of his hod to Joshua (Num 27:20) or when Proverbs warns against giving away one's vigor to strangers (Prov 5:9).

senses.1: The awe-inspiring splendor or majesty associated with God or royalty, often paired with hadar in liturgical and prophetic poetry. Translations across languages converge on 'majesty/splendor' (Ger. Majestaet, Spa. esplendor). Characteristic of divine theophany (Job 37:22) and royal enthronement (1 Chr 29:25), this sense captures the visible radiance of supreme authority.
senses.2: Personal honor, dignity, or distinction belonging to or conferred upon an individual, emphasizing esteem and respect rather than cosmic grandeur. In Num 27:20 Moses gives some of his hod to Joshua as a transfer of authority; in Prov 5:9 it warns against squandering one's vigor or reputation. Daniel 11:21 uses it of royal dignity not rightfully bestowed.

gloss_terse: To be good, pleasant, or pleasing; in causative stems, to do good, act well, or deal generously with someone.
gloss_readable: At its core this verb describes a state of goodness or pleasantness, frequently appearing in the idiom 'to be good in one's eyes' meaning to find approval (Num 24:1; Deut 15:16). Spanish and French translations capture this dual quality well: bueno/bien and bon all orbit around both moral goodness and experiential pleasantness. In its causative usage the focus shifts to active benevolence -- God doing good to His people (Jer 32:41; Ps 119:68) or a person acting rightly before God (1 Kgs 8:18). The German renderings show the semantic breadth, ranging from simple gut to more specific constructions for doing well.

senses.1: Qal stative sense: to be good, pleasant, or agreeable, often in the evaluative idiom 'good in someone's eyes.' Cross-linguistic glosses converge on basic goodness (Eng. good, Spa. bueno, Fra. bon, Ger. gut). Used of things, situations, or conditions being favorable -- Balaam sees it is good in God's eyes to bless Israel (Num 24:1), and the tents of Jacob are called tov (Num 24:5).
senses.2: Hiphil causative sense: to do good, act well, or deal generously with someone. The agent actively brings about goodness. God promises to do good to Israel and rejoice over them (Jer 32:41); the psalmist declares 'You are good and You do good' (Ps 119:68). Translations reflect the causative shift: Spa. Haz bien, hiciste bien; Fra. etre bon with causative markers.

gloss_terse: To be quenched or go out (of fire/lamp); in Piel, to extinguish or put out actively.
gloss_readable: A vivid verb for the dying of fire or light, carrying powerful theological weight. In its intransitive sense it describes a flame going out on its own -- the sacred altar fire that must never be quenched (Lev 6:12-13), or the lamp of God not yet gone out in the sanctuary at Shiloh (1 Sam 3:3). Spanish apagarse and German ausloeschen both capture this self-extinguishing quality. The transitive Piel form introduces an agent who actively puts out the fire, as when David's men protect him lest he 'extinguish the lamp of Israel' (2 Sam 21:17), or when the Song of Songs declares that many waters cannot quench love (Song 8:7).

senses.1: Qal intransitive: of a fire, lamp, or flame ceasing to burn, going out without an agent extinguishing it. Often appears with negation to stress perpetual burning, as in the altar fire commands (Lev 6:12-13). Used prophetically of divine judgment fires that will not be quenched (2 Kgs 22:17; Isa 66:24). Spanish apagarse and German ausloeschen both reflect the self-extinguishing nuance.
senses.2: Piel transitive/causative: to actively quench, extinguish, or put out a fire or lamp, with an explicit or implied agent performing the action. The Chronicler records that the priests had shut up the temple and extinguished the lamps (2 Chr 29:7). Figuratively, the metaphor of 'extinguishing the lamp of Israel' (2 Sam 21:17) warns against losing David in battle. Song 8:7 memorably declares that many waters cannot extinguish love.

gloss_terse: Carmel: (1) the famous mountain promontory on the Mediterranean coast; (2) a town in Judah; (3) as common noun, garden land or fruitful field.
gloss_readable: Most often a place name -- the lush, forested mountain jutting into the Mediterranean where Elijah confronted the prophets of Baal (1 Kgs 18:19-42), or the town in the Judean highlands where Nabal sheared his sheep (1 Sam 25:2). The translations are remarkably consistent across languages: Spa. Carmelo, Fra. Carmel, Ger. Karmel, all preserving the proper noun. Yet the word also functions as a common noun meaning 'garden land' or 'fruitful field,' reflecting the mountain's proverbial fertility. Micah 7:14 plays on both senses, asking God to shepherd His flock in the karmel, evoking both the geographic Carmel and the idea of abundant pasture.

senses.1: The proper noun Carmel, designating either Mount Carmel on the Mediterranean coast (the site of Elijah's contest, 1 Kgs 18:19) or the town of Carmel in the hill country of Judah (1 Sam 25:2). All major language traditions transliterate consistently: Spa. Carmelo, Fra. Carmel, Ger. Karmel. Prophets invoke Carmel alongside Lebanon, Sharon, and Bashan as symbols of the land's richness (Isa 33:9; Jer 50:19).
senses.2: The common noun meaning garden land, fruitful field, or orchard -- reflecting the proverbial fertility of the Carmel region. In 2 Chr 26:10 Uzziah has farmers in the karmel because he loves the soil. Micah 7:14 may deliberately evoke both the place and the metaphor, asking God to shepherd Israel in fertile pasture. Spanish and German sometimes render it as the place name even here, but the context points to agricultural abundance.

gloss_terse: Twisted cords, ropes, or bands for binding; also thick, interwoven boughs or dense branches of a tree.
gloss_readable: A word whose root meaning of 'intertwining' branches into two distinct domains. In its primary sense it refers to twisted or braided ropes and cords -- the fresh ropes binding Samson (Judg 15:13-14), the golden cordage of the priestly ephod (Exod 28:14, 22-25), or the figurative bonds of sin and divine authority (Ps 2:3; Isa 5:18). German Schnur ('cord') and Spanish cuerdas/lazos both confirm this rope-and-binding cluster. The secondary sense describes thick, interwoven branches or dense foliage, appearing exclusively in Ezekiel's tree allegories (Ezek 19:11; 31:3, 10, 14), where the same image of interlacing fibers extends from rope to canopy.

senses.1: Twisted or braided ropes, cords, and bands used for binding, restraining, fastening, or drawing. Covers the literal ropes of the Samson narrative (Judg 15:13-14; 16:11-12), the ornamental cords of the priestly breastpiece (Exod 28:14, 22-25), and figurative bonds of oppression or sin (Ps 2:3; Isa 5:18). Cross-linguistic glosses converge: Ger. Schnur, Spa. cuerdas/cordones, Fra. corde.
senses.2: Thick, interwoven boughs or dense branches of a tree, used of lush foliage and forest canopy. Found exclusively in Ezekiel's prophetic tree allegories: the vine's thick branches (Ezek 19:11) and the great cedar's dense boughs (Ezek 31:3, 10, 14). The semantic thread linking both senses is the root idea of intertwining -- fibers twisted into rope or branches woven into canopy.

gloss_terse: A deed, act, or work (whether of God or humans); also a contrived charge or baseless accusation in legal contexts.
gloss_readable: Primarily denotes actions or deeds, used with striking range. The psalmists celebrate God's mighty alilot -- His awesome works toward humanity (Ps 66:5; 77:12) and His acts made known among the nations (1 Chr 16:8). German Taten and Spanish obras both capture this broad 'deeds' sense. Ezekiel uses the plural repeatedly for Israel's corrupt practices and evil conduct (Ezek 14:22; 20:43; 36:17). A specialized legal sense appears in Deuteronomy 22:14, 17, where it means 'contrived charges' or 'baseless accusations' -- a husband fabricating alilot devarim ('wantonness of words') against his bride. The accusation translations (Eng. accusations, Spa. pretextos) highlight this forensic narrowing.

senses.1: A deed, act, or work performed by God or humans, used broadly for conduct whether praiseworthy or blameworthy. The psalmist declares God's acts among the peoples (1 Chr 16:8 = Ps 105:1), and Ps 66:5 invites onlookers to see His awesome deeds. Ezekiel repeatedly uses the plural for Israel's corrupt practices (Ezek 20:43; 36:17, 19). Multilingual glosses cluster around 'deeds/works': Ger. Taten, Spa. obras, Fra. action.
senses.2: A formal accusation, contrived charge, or pretext brought against someone in a legal setting. Exclusively in Deut 22:14, 17, where a husband brings alilot devarim ('baseless charges') against his bride, claiming she was not a virgin. The forensic specificity is confirmed by translation choices: Eng. accusations, Spa. pretextos, Fra. accusations -- all narrowing from general 'deeds' to deliberate fabrications in a judicial proceeding.
